fields.v: Sharma, R. K. (2026). ContextCov: Bridging the Gap Between Developer Intent and Autonomous Agent Execution. arXiv:2603.00822v2 [cs.SE], 4 May 2026
Preprint — arXiv:2603.00822v2 (4 May 2026), ACM-style layout; no published venue stated (arXiv export has no journal-ref or DOI)
University of Washington, Seattle, USA (single author)

Proposes an approach; secondary: Compares — ContextCov compiles agent instruction files such as AGENTS.md into executable guardrails; compared with two baselines (Vanilla, LLM Reflection) on SWE-bench Lite
ContextCov (no version; code at github.com/reSHARMA/ContextCov). Input artefact: Agent Instruction files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, copilot-instructions.md)

Input: agent instruction file (Markdown). Generated: refined standalone constraints with header path and stable hash IDs; JSON file of executable Python checks in four domains: Process (PATH shell shims blocking prohibited commands), Source (Tree-sitter AST queries), Architectural-Deterministic (NetworkX dependency-graph checks), Architectural-Semantic (LLM-as-judge rubrics, warnings only). Violation traces returned to the agent

Check generation: Markdown AST parse -> path-aware slicing -> LLM refinement of each constraint (gpt-5.2-chat) -> intent router to domain -> expert generators (Claude Code + Opus 4.5) with self-test loop, syntax check and dry run -> JSON of checks. Runtime enforcement: shims intercept commands; static/architectural checks on repo, diff or unstaged changes; violations fed back to the agent for self-correction (max 5 rounds in evaluation). Incremental re-generation when instruction file changes
Developers can review and edit the generated JSON checks before deployment; semantic warnings flagged for human review; false positives resolved by refining the instruction file or marking exceptions
Full workflow of the proposed tool (check generation + runtime enforcement) with generated AGENTS.md files

Not stated in Böckeler terms. Author treats instruction files as 'executable specifications' compiled into enforcement checks ('documentation as code', 'living contract'); closest to spec-anchored (instructions kept and enforced continuously)
fields.why: The author never uses SDD levels; the input is an agent instruction file, not a feature specification. 'Spec-anchored' rests on the author calling instruction files 'executable specifications' and a 'living contract' (p. 1, 9); a reader could equally record 'not classifiable' as for the other context-file studies

Automatic: official SWE-bench Lite harness, executable oracle (ContextCov checks applied post-hoc to the baselines), logged LLM input characters and wall-clock time, McNemar tests. Semi-automatic: blind human annotation of 384 sampled legacy violations (extraction precision); LLM-as-judge (Claude Opus 4.5) for the false-positive analysis, compared with the human annotation (85.42% agreement, kappa 0.61). Post-hoc LLM Reflection critic applied to all final patches. Runtime semantic architectural checks use an LLM-as-judge whose model is not stated

Criterion: SWE-bench Lite tests (resolution) and executable constraint oracle (compliance). All with OpenCode + GPT-5.2 (critic for LLM Reflection: Claude Opus 4.5). One run per task (number of runs not stated). Verdicts judged on each configuration's own values: quality partly when it resolves part but not nearly all tasks; cost from feedback and end-to-end time (no cost threshold set by the author)
- Vanilla (AGENTS.md in context, no feedback) + OpenCode + GPT-5.2 (baseline): resolved 159/300 (53.0%); compliance 201 (67.0%); end-to-end mean 327.9 s (median 184.7). Quality: partly; cost: works
- LLM Reflection + OpenCode + GPT-5.2 (critic Claude Opus 4.5): resolved 157 (52.3%); compliance 151 (50.3%); avg rounds 2.30, 85 hit the 5-round cap (28%); feedback 19,455 chars and 133.7 s mean; end-to-end mean 461.4 s (median 379.2). Quality: partly; cost: partly (heavy-tailed feedback cost, 28% of tasks exhaust the round budget)
- ContextCov + OpenCode + GPT-5.2: resolved 172 (57.3%); compliance 265 (88.3%); avg rounds 1.31, 29 hit cap (10%); feedback 6,292 chars and 27.7 s mean; end-to-end mean 422.4 s (median 240.0). Quality: partly (high compliance, resolution 57.3%); cost: works
fields.why: Verdicts were set relative to the baselines and the Vanilla baseline had none; draft-verify and §6 require each configuration, baseline included, to be judged on its own. Verdicts redone from each configuration's own values (Tables 2, 3, 5, p. 7-8); ContextCov quality lowered from works to partly because 42.7% of tasks stay unresolved; thresholds are the extractor's. LLM Reflection end-to-end time and medians added from Table 5

fields.v: Tasks: SWE-bench Lite (300), with AGENTS.md files generated by a few-shot LLM from existing repo docs, lint configs and CI files. Configurations: Vanilla, LLM Reflection, ContextCov. Baselines: Vanilla and LLM Reflection. Held constant: agent scaffold (OpenCode), coding model (GPT-5.2), instruction files, 5-round feedback budget for both feedback methods. Acceptance tests: official SWE-bench harness; compliance via ContextCov's own oracle (post-hoc for baselines). Repetitions: Not stated (one run per task apparently). Human intervention: none during runs

ContextCov best: resolution 57.3% vs 53.0% Vanilla (+4.3 pts, McNemar p=0.031; discordant 22/9) and 52.3% LLM Reflection (+5.0, p=0.046); Vanilla vs LLM Reflection n.s. (p=0.885). Compliance 88.3% vs 67.0% vs 50.3%. Feedback cost ~3x lower and latency ~80% lower than LLM Reflection; 3.4x higher cost-efficiency. Residual ContextCov violations only source-level

Distinguished the configurations on resolution and compliance. Repeatability: code and results released; number of runs not stated (apparently one); no multiplicity correction (stated). Limitations stated by the author: generated instruction files may not match maintainer intent; single LLM-judge configuration; SWE-bench Lite only (12 Python-heavy repos); subgroup analyses may be underpowered. Not stated by the author (reviewer observation): compliance is measured with ContextCov's own checks, applied post-hoc to the baselines, which favours the approach

False positives from LLM misinterpretation, overly strict checks or implicit exceptions; generated instruction files may not match maintainer intent; single LLM-judge configuration; SWE-bench Lite only (12 Python-heavy repos, 300 tasks); subgroup analyses underpowered; McNemar tests without multiplicity correction; replication on other benchmarks needed

Code and evaluation results: https://github.com/reSHARMA/ContextCov. Table 1 (per-repository) jumbled by pdftotext; totals rebuilt (1,498 lines, 665 segments, 241 source / 296 process / 158 arch-deterministic / 93 arch-semantic = 788 checks). Reporting inconsistencies: abstract claims '3.4x lower feedback cost', while the body gives ~3x lower feedback cost (19,455 vs 6,292 chars) and 3.4x higher cost-efficiency (p. 8); '780/781' Python checks parsed (p. 6) does not match 788 checks of which 93 are semantic rubrics, not Python; Figure 4 caption labels 'RQ5' and 'Self-Reflection' (= LLM Reflection). Compliance oracle is the proposed tool itself applied post-hoc to baselines. Motivating scenarios based on informal probing. No pre-registration.
